blocks.text: The handbill reached Jenny’s desk before the morning assignments did. Eleanor Blackwell’s name filled the top. Beneath it, in heavier print, were two words: FREE ELECTRICITY.
Jenny read the smaller lines. A neighborhood meeting that afternoon. A new energy proposal for Cleveland. No account of how it would work.
Her editor stopped beside the desk. “Get there early. I want to know whether she means free or whether somebody else gets the bill.”
Jenny tucked the handbill into her notebook. “So do I.”

By the time she reached the meeting hall, most of the folding chairs were occupied. A woman near the front had brought an electricity bill. She smoothed it against her knee while the man beside her counted something on his fingers.

Jenny found a place in the aisle. She had expected campaign workers and a few reporters. There were parents with small children, elderly couples and shopkeepers still wearing their work clothes. An aide carried in more chairs.

Eleanor arrived in her black suit, silver curls untouched by the wind outside. Her dark glasses stayed on as she stepped onto the low platform. She thanked the people who had come, waited for a child to stop coughing, and rested both hands on the lectern.
“I’ve heard what it costs you to keep your homes running,” she said. “The lights. The refrigerator. The shop you’ve worked all your life to keep open.”
The woman with the bill looked up.
“Cleveland deserves better than another promise to look into it.” Eleanor paused. “If you elect me mayor, I will bring free electricity to this city.”

Applause started in the front row and spread. A man near Jenny stood to clap. Eleanor waited behind the microphone, smiling, while people turned to one another as though the next bill might already be different.
blocks.alt: Eleanor Blackwell promises free electricity at a Cleveland neighborhood meeting in 1987. Residents applaud while civilian reporter Jenny Jenkins takes notes in the aisle.

blocks.text: Jenny wrote the promise exactly. Beside it, she left space for how.

Eleanor spoke about money left over for groceries, businesses able to hire, and streetlights the city could afford to keep burning. She never named a power station. She never said what would produce the electricity.
When she invited questions, the woman at the front raised her bill.
“Would that include my apartment? I don’t own the building.”
“My intention is to reach every household,” Eleanor said.
The woman lowered the page slowly. “That would make a difference.”
Jenny waited for a question about a neighborhood bakery, then lifted her hand.
“Jenny Jenkins, the Defender. Where will the electricity come from?”
Eleanor’s smile held. “A new source of energy. The people developing it believe it could meet Cleveland’s needs without the fuel costs we pay now.”
“Who are the people developing it?”
“I’ll introduce the technical team when the work is ready.”
“Has it powered anything yet?”
A chair scraped behind Jenny. Eleanor glanced toward the sound, then back at her.
“The research is progressing.”
“How much electricity has it produced?”
“I haven’t brought laboratory figures to a neighborhood meeting, Miss Jenkins.”
Jenny kept her notebook open. “Could your office send them to the paper? And the name of someone independent who has checked them?”
blocks.alt: Jenny Jenkins, in her white blouse and pink skirt, questions Eleanor Blackwell about her electricity proposal as residents turn to listen in a neighborhood meeting hall.

blocks.text: “There will be proper checks before anything is connected.” Eleanor lifted a hand toward the room. “I wouldn’t ask these families to accept something unsafe.”
“Then it hasn’t passed those checks yet?”
An aide moved toward the microphone. Eleanor stopped him with a small gesture.
“I’m announcing what I intend to deliver as mayor. The work is still being completed.”
Jenny wrote that down beneath free electricity.
“Who pays for the equipment and the people running it?” she asked. “Would the money come from city taxes?”
“We’re working through the arrangements. Private support has helped us get this far.”
“Whose support?”

“I will release the details when there is a complete proposal to show you. Today, I wanted the people of Cleveland to hear what we’re working toward.” Eleanor looked beyond Jenny. “There’s a gentleman at the back who’s been waiting.”
Jenny lowered her hand. Around her, some people were still smiling. Others had stopped clapping. The woman with the electricity bill folded it and put it in her handbag.
After the meeting, Jenny caught up with her beside the stacked chairs.
“Do you think she can do it?” the woman asked.
“I don’t know yet,” Jenny said. “She hasn’t shown us how.”
The woman glanced toward the platform, where Eleanor was shaking hands. “I’d like her to be right.”
“So would I.” Jenny looked down at the notebook. “May I ask you what a month’s electricity costs you?”

She stayed to hear the answer. Then she spoke to a bakery owner and a retired man who had written down Eleanor’s promise on the back of his bus timetable. None of them needed convincing that free electricity would help. They wanted to know when they could have it.

Back at the Defender, Jenny telephoned Eleanor’s campaign office. She requested the output figures, the equipment costs and the names of the people responsible for the research. The woman who took the message said someone would get back to her.
Billy arrived while Jenny was arranging her notes. He read the handbill she slid across the desk.
“A new source,” he said.
“That’s as much as she would tell us.” Jenny showed him her questions. “She’s asking people to believe it before she’s shown that it works.”
Billy tapped the words private support. “She paid Daniel’s laboratory bills. That doesn’t prove he’s behind this.”
“No,” Jenny said. “But I’m asking who is.”
Billy opened his notebook. “I’ll keep following the order that held back the police. You find out what she’s promising to connect to the city.”

At her typewriter, Jenny began with Eleanor’s announcement. She included what it would mean to the people in the hall. Then she set down the unanswered questions and the campaign’s promise to supply details.

Outside the newsroom window, the afternoon faded. Lamps came on in the offices across the street, one floor after another. Jenny watched them for a moment, then returned to her page. Before Eleanor could ask the city to depend on her new source, somebody needed to find it.
